ChaaS primarily manages risks associated with ownership of EVSE assets. EVSE can lose value for a variety of reasons (repair, abuse, neglect, natural disaster), but a key reason is potential obsolescence. For midlevel (50-350 kW) charging, competing charging connector standards exist (Tesla, SAE). The future viability of each of these standards is uncertain and will depend on economic outcomes and/or policy decisions. Already, many standards have been discontinued (including CHAdeMO, AVCON, and Magne Charge) and, in the European Union, steps have been taken toward unifying connector standards for public charging. Furthermore, standards for high-level (≥1 MW) charging of commercial vehicles are being developed, but have yet to be published. Thus, adopters of EV charging face the risk that the connector style they adopt may become obsolete in the near or long term (obsolescence risk). Further, the charging rates of which EVSE are capable have increased rapidly over time, presenting a slightly different type of obsolescence risk. Even if connector standards remain unchanged, an adopter of EVSE in the present faces the risk that higher-power EVSE, which may be more profitable or operationally suitable, may become available in the future. This would leave them “locked in” with slower and less suitable equipment (lock-in risk). By allowing a risk-tolerant ChaaS provider to bear the costs and responsibilities of EVSE ownership, a risk-averse EV adopter 16 Bradley, T.H., et al., Agent-Based, Bottom-Up Medium- and Heavy-duty Electric Vehicle Economics, Operation, Charging and Adoption, Final Technical Report, DE-EE0009664 can avoid the risks of obsolescence and lock-in. EVSE may also become unexpectedly costly to own. EVSE has earned a reputation for unreliability38, which can lead to high unplanned maintenance and/or replacement costs (in addition to disrupting operations). Fueling costs also have long- and short-term variability. Electricity prices can vary drastically with supply and demand, depending on how prices are structured, resulting in short-term price risks for which EV operators may not be accustomed to prepare. While not as volatile as gasoline and diesel prices, long-term changes in electricity prices are influenced by a similar range of unpredictable factors (global politics, technological breakthroughs), making them difficult to predict and creating long- term price risks. ChaaS providers can manage usage cost risks by enforcing variability limits on the usage costs paid by their customers. Such limits could take various forms, but all would actively serve to manage the ownership/operation costs of charging. ChaaS can also function to reduce or defer costs for customers. The costs to procure charging infrastructure can be prohibitively high, regardless of a potential adopter’s risk tolerance. ChaaS functions to offload ownership responsibilities, one of which is to pay or finance the up- front system costs, in exchange for fees incurred over time. This deferment of up-front equipment costs may make EV adoption economically favorable for some customers.
